metadata.name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD/GORD)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine — but red-flag symptoms (dysphagia, GI bleeding, weight loss) require urgent work-up; consider cardiac cause for chest pain
metadata.severity: Usually mild-moderate and manageable; can cause oesophagitis, stricture, and Barrett's oesophagus (premalignant) if severe/chronic

overview.short_description: Troublesome symptoms and/or mucosal damage caused by reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus, classically heartburn and acid regurgitation.
overview.detailed_description: GERD is one of the most common upper-GI conditions in primary care. It exists on a spectrum from non-erosive reflux disease (normal endoscopy) to erosive oesophagitis and complications (stricture, Barrett's oesophagus). Diagnosis in typical cases is clinical, and a therapeutic trial of acid suppression is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Investigation (endoscopy, pH studies) is reserved for red flags, atypical/refractory presentations, or Barrett's surveillance.
overview.pathophysiology: Reflux occurs when the anti-reflux barrier fails: transient lower-oesophageal-sphincter relaxations, low LOS tone, hiatus hernia, impaired oesophageal acid clearance, delayed gastric emptying, and raised intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy). Refluxed acid/pepsin (and sometimes bile) injures oesophageal mucosa and stimulates sensory nerves, producing symptoms and, with chronicity, metaplasia (Barrett's).
overview.etiology: Multifactorial: hiatus hernia, obesity, pregnancy, dietary and lifestyle factors, smoking, certain drugs (see risk factors), and conditions delaying gastric emptying. Helicobacter pylori is not a cause of GERD (and may be inversely related in some patients).
overview.natural_history: Often chronic/relapsing; many controlled with lifestyle and intermittent or continuous acid suppression. A minority progress to erosive disease, stricture, or Barrett's oesophagus (small annual risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma).
overview.prognosis: Generally good; symptom control is achievable in most. Prognosis worsens with long-standing severe disease and Barrett's/dysplasia.

prevalence.value: ~10-20% of adults in Western populations report weekly reflux symptoms; common worldwide and rising with obesity.

incidence.value: Very common presenting complaint in primary care.

mortality.value: Very low directly; relevance is via oesophageal adenocarcinoma risk in Barrett's oesophagus.

epidemiology.age_groups: Any age; prevalence increases with age; also common in pregnancy.
epidemiology.sex_predominance: Roughly equal for symptoms; erosive disease and Barrett's/adenocarcinoma more common in men.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; higher symptom prevalence in Western/high-obesity populations.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Large/late meals, lying down after eating, trigger foods (fatty/spicy, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, citrus, carbonated/alcoholic drinks).
risk_factors.smoking: Lowers LOS tone and worsens reflux; cessation helps.
risk_factors.alcohol: Relaxes LOS and irritates mucosa; worsens symptoms.
risk_factors.obesity: Strong risk factor (raised intra-abdominal pressure, hiatus hernia); weight loss improves symptoms.
risk_factors.hypertension: Not directly related (some antihypertensives e.g. calcium-channel blockers can worsen reflux).
risk_factors.pregnancy: Common cause (hormonal LOS relaxation + mechanical pressure); usually resolves postpartum.
risk_factors.occupation: Jobs involving bending/heavy lifting may aggravate.
risk_factors.medications: Calcium-channel blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics, theophylline, bisphosphonates, NSAIDs (mucosal injury), some sedatives — can cause or worsen reflux/oesophagitis.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Hiatus hernia, scleroderma (oesophageal dysmotility), prior gastric surgery.

symptoms.symptom: Heartburn (retrosternal burning, worse after meals/lying down)
Symptoms worse lying flat/bending or at night, relieved by antacids
Chronic cough / hoarseness / laryngitis / dental erosion (extra-oesophageal)

symptoms.importance: RED FLAG - suggests stricture or malignancy; needs endoscopy

negative_findings.finding: No dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, anaemia, GI bleeding, or vomiting
negative_findings.why_important: Absence of alarm features supports uncomplicated GERD and empirical therapy without urgent endoscopy

negative_findings.finding: Pain not exertional and not relieved by rest/GTN
negative_findings.why_important: Reduces (but does not exclude) cardiac cause of chest pain

history_questions.question: Do you get burning behind the breastbone or acid coming up, especially after meals or lying down?
Any difficulty or pain swallowing, food sticking, weight loss, black stools, vomiting blood, or persistent vomiting?
Is the chest discomfort brought on by exertion and relieved by rest?
history_questions.why_ask: Distinguishes cardiac chest pain from reflux

history_questions.question: What triggers it (foods, alcohol, large/late meals), and does it wake you at night?
Do you take NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, calcium-channel blockers, or steroids?
history_questions.why_ask: Drugs that cause/worsen reflux or oesophageal injury

history_questions.question: Have you tried antacids/alginates and did they help?
history_questions.why_ask: Response supports reflux and guides therapy

physical_examination.examination: Cardiovascular/respiratory exam if chest pain or atypical symptoms
physical_examination.importance: High if chest pain (exclude cardiac/respiratory cause)

laboratory_tests.indication: If anaemia/bleeding suspected or alarm features
laboratory_tests.expected_result: Usually normal; microcytic anaemia suggests chronic GI blood loss
laboratory_tests.diagnostic_value: Detects complications, not diagnostic of GERD

laboratory_tests.test_name: Helicobacter pylori testing (stool antigen or urea breath test)
laboratory_tests.indication: Dyspepsia overlap / before long-term PPI in some pathways
laboratory_tests.diagnostic_value: Guides eradication in dyspepsia (H. pylori does not cause GERD)

imaging.imaging_type: Barium swallow (rarely, e.g. suspected stricture/hiatus hernia if endoscopy unsuitable)

ecg.when_needed: If chest pain could be cardiac
ecg.findings: Normal in GERD; used to help exclude ischaemia (does not fully exclude — clinical judgement/cardiac work-up as needed).

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Upper GI endoscopy (OGD): indicated for alarm features, age/risk-based new dyspepsia, refractory symptoms, or Barrett's surveillance. May show oesophagitis (Los Angeles grade), stricture, or Barrett's; often normal in non-erosive reflux disease.
other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Oesophageal biopsy if Barrett's/eosinophilic oesophagitis/malignancy suspected at endoscopy.

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Primarily clinical in typical cases: troublesome heartburn and/or acid regurgitation. A positive response to a PPI trial supports the diagnosis. Objective confirmation (when needed) is by endoscopy (erosive oesophagitis/Barrett's) or ambulatory 24-hour oesophageal pH (+/- impedance) monitoring showing abnormal acid exposure (e.g., % time pH <4 above threshold).
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: Symptom questionnaires (e.g., GERD-Q) can aid diagnosis and monitoring; not required.

cutoff_values.value: Ambulatory pH: abnormal oesophageal acid exposure typically defined as acid exposure time >6% (Lyon consensus); LA-grade C/D oesophagitis is diagnostic of GERD.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Exertional, radiates to arm/jaw, associated dyspnoea/sweating
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it triggered by exertion and relieved by rest?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Epigastric pain, hunger/night pain, H. pylori/NSAID related
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_symptoms: Epigastric pain rather than burning behind sternum
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the pain more in the stomach and related to hunger?
Do you have allergies and food sticking?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Alarm features: progressive dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia, older age
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any trouble swallowing or weight loss?

differential_diagnosis.differences: RUQ pain after fatty meals, radiating to back/shoulder
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the pain right-sided after fatty food?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your chest discomfort brought on by exertion and relieved by rest, or is it burning after meals/lying down?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Exertional -> assess cardiac urgently; postprandial burning -> supports reflux

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have progressive difficulty swallowing or unintentional weight loss?

next_best_question.current_situation: Typical heartburn, no alarm features, age-appropriate
next_best_question.question: Would you like to try lifestyle changes plus a course of acid-suppressing medication and review response?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Improves -> confirms/treats GERD, step down; No improvement -> reassess, consider endoscopy/pH study/other diagnosis

next_best_question.question: Any exertional component, breathlessness, sweating, or radiation to arm/jaw?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Yes -> cardiac pathway first; No -> reflux pathway

next_best_test.why: Diagnostic and therapeutic in typical cases without alarm features
Alarm features, refractory symptoms, or Barrett's surveillance
next_best_test.expected_outcome: Identifies oesophagitis, stricture, Barrett's, or malignancy

next_best_test.why: Confirm reflux when diagnosis uncertain or before anti-reflux surgery, especially with normal endoscopy

red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent upper GI endoscopy referral (suspected stricture/malignancy)

red_flags.finding: Unintentional weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, or upper GI bleeding (haematemesis/melaena)
red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent (2-week-wait) endoscopy / acute assessment if active bleeding

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with exertional features / cardiac risk
red_flags.immediate_action: Assess for acute coronary syndrome before attributing to reflux

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anaemia, mass, persistent vomiting) — urgent/2-week-wait endoscopy; Barrett's with dysplasia.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Refractory symptoms despite optimised therapy, diagnostic uncertainty, consideration of anti-reflux surgery, Barrett's surveillance.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Active haematemesis/melaena with haemodynamic compromise; suspected acute coronary syndrome.

early: Sleep disturbance, reduced quality of life
late: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma (small long-term risk via Barrett's)
Dental erosion, chronic laryngitis, aspiration/asthma exacerbation

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance and explanation; identify and address triggers; assess for alarm features first.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Proton-pump inhibitor; H2-receptor antagonist; Antacid/alginate. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_CG184.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Weight loss if overweight, smaller and earlier evening meals, avoid trigger foods/alcohol/caffeine, stop smoking, raise the head of the bed, avoid lying down within ~3 hours of eating.
initial_management.follow_up: Review symptom response after the initial PPI course; step-down therapy; re-evaluate or investigate if no response, relapse on stopping, or new alarm features.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Antacids/alginates for immediate/intermittent relief; proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) for 4-8 weeks as first-line for troublesome symptoms/oesophagitis, then step down to lowest effective dose or on-demand; H2-receptor antagonist as alternative/add-on. Review and stop/avoid aggravating drugs where possible. Long-term/maintenance PPI for erosive oesophagitis or relapse; use lowest effective dose.

patient_education.home_advice: Reflux is common and usually manageable. Eat smaller, earlier meals, avoid your trigger foods, alcohol and smoking, lose extra weight, and raise the head of your bed. Antacids help quickly; acid-reducing tablets help over weeks. See a doctor promptly if you have trouble swallowing, weight loss, black stools, or vomit blood.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: الارتجاع شائع ويمكن التحكم به عادةً. تناول وجبات أصغر وأبكر، وتجنّب الأطعمة المهيّجة والكحول والتدخين، وأنقِص الوزن الزائد، وارفع رأس السرير. مضادات الحموضة تريح بسرعة، وأدوية تقليل الحمض تفيد خلال أسابيع. راجع الطبيب فوراً إذا صعُب البلع أو نقص وزنك أو صار البراز أسود أو تقيّأت دماً.
patient_education.prevention: Weight control, avoiding late/large meals and known triggers, not smoking.
patient_education.warning_signs: Difficulty or pain on swallowing, food sticking, unintentional weight loss, black/tarry stools, vomiting blood, or exertional chest pain — seek prompt medical review.

prevention.lifestyle: Weight management, dietary modification, smoking cessation, meal timing.
prevention.screening: No population screening for GERD; endoscopic surveillance for diagnosed Barrett's oesophagus.

evidence.evidence_level: High for PPI efficacy and lifestyle measures (RCTs and systematic reviews).
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_CG184; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong — NICE CG184, ACG, BMJ Best Practice; Lyon consensus for objective diagnosis.
